title.narrative: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) core contributions 2022-23 to 2025-26

description.narrative:
The Australia - World Food Programme Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) sets the objectives and obligations for partnership. It outlines the parameters for Australia's global funding, and the requirements for any subsidiary arrangements that will direct funding to specific crises/programmes.
This investment delivers Australia's core funding contributions under the current Strategic Partnership Framework.

participating-org.narrative: AUSTRALIA - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

organisation.narrative: Australia - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

description.narrative: Australia’s 2022 core funding to WFP contributed to the scale up of anticipatory actions to reach 1.7 million people, enlarging the scope of those actions to cover tropical cyclones and using innovative approaches to respond to the needs of people ahead of climate shocks. In nine countries, 460,000 people received USD 8.7 million in anticipatory cash-based transfers together with early warning messaging aimed at mitigating the impacts of predicted droughts and floods.

Australia’s core funding to WFP supports the resilience of communities by tackling the underlying drivers of food insecurity. In 2022, WFP assisted approximately 10 million people through asset creation and livelihood activities, almost 3.4 million people through climate risk insurance or anticipatory actions and nearly 845,000 people through its smallholder agricultural market support programmes. WFP’s activities included restoring land, water and other productive assets. WFP also supported smallholder farmers to increase their access to markets. Australia’s core funding to WFP also enables communities to adapt to climate change and protect their livelihoods through access to insurance and tailored weather forecasts.

In 2023 nine out of ten Afghans lacked adequate food, with food costing 89% of household incomes, leaving families struggling to feed their children. ‍ Particularly hard hit were women, whose income opportunities shrank due to restrictions on women’s mobility. ‍ “Me and my husband both lost our work,” Basira, a 45-year-old mother of six said when she picked up wheat flour, cooking oil, peas and salt at a distribution site in Mazar-e-Sharif. “He went to Iran to find work as a day labourer but the money he sends me is not enough to cover even our most basic needs.” ‍ Basira was one of 13 million people across Afghanistan who received food assistance in early 2023 — over 80 percent of whom were women and children. ‍ In 2023, WFP allocated 11 per cent of Australia's core funding to Afghanistan. In addition, Australia contributed a further $16 million towards WFP’s operations in Afghanistan.

In 2024, Australia’s support to the World Food Programme (WFP) enabled life-saving humanitarian assistance across multiple emergencies, reaching over 90 million people. This included the delivery of 2.2 million metric tonnes of food and $1.7 billion in cash assistance and vouchers. ‍ Australia contributed to WFP responses to 31 emergencies, including in Myanmar, Afghanistan, Yemen, Sudan, and South Sudan. WFP’s supply chain played a central role in ensuring the timely delivery of food, cash assistance (responsive to essential needs), and other essential relief to hard-to-reach and conflict-affected areas. ‍ In Bangladesh, extreme weather events such as Cyclone Remal disproportionately impacted food-insecure communities. WFP scaled up its existing food security response, exceeding planned cash transfer targets and reaching more beneficiaries than anticipated, thanks in part to Australia's support. These efforts helped mitigate the impact of climate shocks and ensured those most in need received rapid assistance.
